comparator.name: Sociology
comparator.sourceNotes: Current dated programme 5890/41082, electives 40601, progression 40602 and individual 2026–2027 course entries establish a complete 180-EC ordinary pathway: 60 compulsory first-year credits, 60 compulsory second-year credits, 30 genuinely open elective credits and 30 final research/method/policy credits. Retain the English language pathway; the bilingual pathway has the same academic content and differs in tutorial and assessment language. The current catalogue and transition table replace the four historical introduction, critical-theory, intersectionality and urban titles; no old/new duplicate is counted. Ordinary completion of the prior year satisfies the documented 42-credit second-year conditions, Statistics/Amsterdam-project prerequisites and final 108-credit first/second-year threshold including Advanced Statistics and Qualitative Analysis. Mixed Methods requires 60 Sociology credits including Advanced Statistics; Public Policy requires 60 Sociology credits. The eighteen-credit Bachelor Research Project covers the empirical cycle in supervised small groups and is individually assessed through the bachelor thesis. The open elective space remains uninstantiated, with course-entry/registration conditions; no optional honours, internship or restricted example is made compulsory. No material formal conflict remains requiring an additional OER search.
components: Reading and sociological reasoning prepare for Sociology as Craft 2, which develops the academic literature review and writing.
Introduction to Sociology: Concepts, Issues and Research
Introduces quantitative, qualitative and mixed research and hands-on surveys; the collected data are used in Introduction to Statistics.

A short intensive qualitative project uses observation and interviewing, research ethics and a student-conference presentation. Prior participation in Social Research Methodology is strongly recommended.
Ordinary second-year progression requires 42 first-year Sociology credits. The domain examines how schooling and work reproduce or challenge inequalities.
Race, Gender, and Sexuality in Times of Fascism
Requires 42 first-year Sociology credits. Studies intersecting race, gender and sexuality through epistemology, political economy and contemporary fascist forces.
Requires 42 first-year Sociology credits. Examines migration, citizenship and political, structural, social and cultural integration.

Requires 42 first-year Sociology credits and introductory statistics and quantitative research methods. Studies population health, social determinants and health inequalities.
Sociological Theory 3: Society, Social Action and Inequality
Requires 42 first-year Sociology credits. Compares macro- and micro-level accounts of social action and inequality.
Requires 42 first-year Sociology credits. Studies cultural globalisation, colonial power, oppression and transnational resistance.
Requires 42 first-year Sociology credits. Studies how cultural meanings and social structures interact in contemporary theory.
Complete 42 first-year Sociology credits, including the Amsterdam Research Project. Develops coding, thematic and discourse analysis and reflexive qualitative inquiry.

Thirty credits remain genuinely open for eligible electives, a minor, study abroad or a combination including an optional internship. Check each chosen course’s level, entry conditions and registration. No particular package or internship is compulsory.
Complete 60 Sociology credits including Advanced Statistics. Develops the epistemological and practical integration of qualitative and quantitative methods, alongside the final research project.
Complete 60 Sociology credits. Studies the institutional, political and social processes of policy development, implementation and evaluation.

Before this eighteen-credit project starts, at least 108 first- and second-year Sociology credits must be completed and registered, including Advanced Statistics and Qualitative Analysis. Small-group supervision and feedback support an individual bachelor thesis covering the empirical research cycle. Select a project from the offered research groups; no particular topic is guaranteed.

alternatives.label: Sociology, inequality & social research
alternatives.concept: Build a sociological study of inequality and social change through classical, modern and civil-society theory. Qualitative inquiry, statistical modelling, data analysis, health evidence and historical research connect institutions, identity and public problems to empirical investigation.
alternatives.labelReason: Build a sociological study of inequality and social change through classical, modern and civil-society theory. progression: All formal prerequisites precede their courses and all assigned terms have planned offerings. Introductory sociology precedes modern and advanced theory; methods precede courses with that formal prerequisite, including public/international economics, econometrics and the supervised leadership survey. PPD is in the first year. Each programme has at least six advanced courses.

alternatives.label: Institutions, policy & collective action
alternatives.concept: Investigate how legal, political and economic institutions shape inequality and collective responses to public problems. Sociology, public economics, governance, rights and communication connect policy choices to social movements, inclusion and research.
alternatives.labelReason: Investigate how legal, political and economic institutions shape inequality and collective responses to public problems. Sociology, public economics, governance, rights and communication connect policy choices to social movements, inclusion and research.
alternatives.distinctness: Replaces historical, health and general statistical/data priorities with constitutional and private law, public economics, governance and policy communication. Consumer-product design is replaced by actual public-economics content, sharpening the institutional and distributive purpose.

alternatives.label: Race, gender & global social relations
alternatives.concept: Investigate racial and gendered power, identity and global social relations through sociology, imperial and Indigenous histories, cultural exchange and international institutions. Qualitative and historical research connect these structures to lived experience, collective action and educational inclusion.
alternatives.labelReason: Investigate racial and gendered power, identity and global social relations through sociology, imperial and Indigenous histories, cultural exchange and international institutions. alternatives.distinctness: Emphasises imperial and Indigenous histories, gender, race, cultural exchange, international relations and educational inclusion rather than domestic legal governance or the broader statistical-health spine. Public Policy Analysis replaces a partner-dependent sustainability project. Dedicated migration and urban sociology remain limitations rather than being inferred from these courses.

courses: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory

core: Sociological theories of social interaction, institutions, culture, structure and social change
Social inequality across class, race, gender, migration, education, work, health and urban life
Qualitative, quantitative and mixed social research using interviews, ethnography, surveys, statistics and critical evidence assessment
Relationships between individuals, everyday interaction, organisations and wider social structures
Academic sociological craft, theory construction and independent research culminating in a thesis
adjacent: Public policy, social movements and collective responses to societal problems
Migration, citizenship, racism, globalisation and identities shaped by urban and transnational settings
Social organisation of education, work, health and culture
questions: What social structures and mechanisms produce inequality and changing public problems?
How do institutions, policies and collective action reproduce or change social relations?
How can qualitative and quantitative evidence explain social patterns and change?

Complementary microeconomic choice, markets, strategic interaction and macroeconomic foundations for analysing institutions and economic conditions behind inequality.
Complementary open-economy growth, labour-market and fiscal/monetary analysis for the economic structures connecting societies; not dedicated migration studies.
Direct distributive and institutional policy analysis through public goods, externalities, taxation, public spending, welfare, education and health, with economic evidence and a research paper.

Direct regression, causal/predictive inference, OLS/GLS/IV and statistical testing in Stata, with Monte Carlo simulations and an empirical paper; economic applications rather than a sociology methods duplicate.
Direct empirical research design, operationalisation, survey/experimental methods, inference and regression, including original team data collection and ethical reporting.

Direct study of psychological safety, belonging, minority experiences and inclusive leadership, with original supervised survey data and statistical reporting; not a complete sociology of education/work.
Direct R data cleaning, visualisation and tabular/text/spatial analysis with a student research question; no unsupported social-network-analysis specialisation.
Direct collective-action, institutions, power, justice, stakeholder and governance analysis of sustainability problems, with policy advice/evaluation.
Direct socio-legal study of law, social control/change and justice with race/gender, institutional cases and a small research proposal.
Direct intersectional gender/sexuality history in North America, including racialised power, queer lives, oral history and community-engaged research.
Direct comparative imperial histories, legitimacy, economic systems, culture and colonial legacies, with independently developed historical inquiry; complementary to contemporary global sociology.
Direct Indigenous history of colonial institutions, family separation, gendered violence, cultural resistance and reciprocity through collaborative public-history inquiry.

Direct research-question development, critical source inquiry, interdisciplinary method and a substantial historical paper in Researching the American Century; not the excluded historical Walcheren outline.
Complementary legal/philosophical human-rights arguments, universalism, statelessness and rights protection for evaluating unequal power and inclusion.
Complementary international-law institutions, self-determination, rights and treaty politics for analysing global legal relations; not a dedicated citizenship/integration course.
Complementary comparative constitutional/administrative analysis of power, rights, participation and remedies in public institutions.
Complementary property, tort, contract and dispute-resolution analysis of rights and obligations in everyday private relations; no claimed family/housing specialisation.
Direct comparative analysis of political institutions, participation, populism, democracy and inequality-relevant political economy, with empirical research.
Complementary IR theories, colonial relations, North–South economic connections and global political cases, with researched international negotiation.
Direct EU institutions, interest representation and policy processes, including empirical amendment coding and legislative research.
Direct public-policy phases and alternative conceptualisations across national/international arenas through a global sugar case and policy memos.
Direct interdisciplinary study of structural inequality, identity, colonial legacies, forced migration and conflict, with evidence-based policy research and positionality reflection.
Direct sociological imagination, classical theories, institutions, social boundaries, class/race/gender, migration and work/education inequalities; theory-led literature research.
Direct qualitative design, interviews, observation, reflexivity, coding and thematic interpretation, with original team research; mixed-method foundations do not equal a dedicated integration course.
Direct critical and modern social theories, Frankfurt School, Black feminism, Bourdieu, coloniality and empirical sociological interpretation.
Direct social-movement theories and environmental-justice cases with feminist, anticolonial, degrowth and environmental-peacebuilding perspectives.
Direct civil-society theory through critical, neo-functionalist and decolonial approaches, trust, solidarity, movements and public spheres, applied in a research project.
Direct population-health evidence, social/environmental determinants, health inequalities, epidemiological methods and a local needs-assessment/intervention project.
Complementary group processes, social cognition, prejudice and social influence for understanding interaction and identity; the final project proposes rather than executes a study.
Direct experimental design and multivariable statistical analysis, diagnostics, R/SPSS practice and empirical reporting for social/behavioural evidence.

Direct educational inclusion, school belonging, youth radicalisation and civic agency through evidence-based teacher/youth resources and recipient feedback; not a general migration/political-psychology curriculum.
Direct study of contested climate communication across public texts/media/protest art and arguments, with a project entering the debate.
Direct ethical persuasion, framing and community sustainability communication, with literature, field diaries and reflective action research.
Complementary specific Renaissance Mediterranean art study of trade, colonisation and cross-cultural production connecting Europe, Africa, Asia and the Americas; not general migration training.
Direct study of racial construction, power, exclusion and resistance in American media/culture, with archival, participant-observation, podcast and cross-cultural narrative inquiry.
blocks: Sociological theory, social relations and empirical inquiry

Both develop critical academic reading, arguments, reflection and study practice. UvA specifically trains the sociological imagination and analysis of sociological texts; UCR also develops writing and community collaboration.
Both develop software-based multiple-regression analysis and interpretation of evidence. UCR additionally treats econometric estimators, simulation, causal inference and an empirical economic paper.

Both develop research questions, operationalisation, survey methods and standards for empirical inquiry. UCR combines this with statistics and a team data project; UvA feeds its survey evidence into the subsequent statistics course.

Both examine unequal experiences and inclusion in organisations and working life. UCR develops psychological safety and minority inclusion through leadership and original survey research; UvA additionally centres schooling and the reproduction of educational and labour-market inequality.

Both examine institutions, social control and change through power and social relations. UCR centres law and justice; UvA more widely studies legitimacy, institutional reproduction and crisis across organisations.

Both connect global cultural and institutional relations to colonial power and its legacies. UCR approaches these through comparative imperial history; UvA directly studies contemporary cultural globalisation and transnational resistance.

Both develop research questions, critical reading and an independently argued academic paper. UCR works through historical sources and a substantial American Century research paper; UvA specifically develops sociological literature-review and writing skills.

Both examine policy formation, institutions, competing interests and how public problems are framed across national and international settings. UCR uses a global sugar case and policy memos; UvA studies sociological explanations across several policy fields.

Both introduce sociological concepts, social institutions, inequality and the analysis of contemporary problems through theory and research. The UvA component is larger and explicitly develops its Netherlands-focused and cross-cultural introduction.

Both develop qualitative coding, reflexivity, thematic interpretation and reporting. UCR additionally follows design and data collection through a team project; UvA explicitly includes thematic and discourse-analysis inquiry.
Both study critical sociological theory, including Marxist and Frankfurt School traditions. UCR additionally foregrounds modernity, colonialism, Black feminism and other theoretical approaches.

Both use contrasting social theories to examine social action, institutions and inequality. UCR concentrates on civil society, solidarity, public spheres and movements; UvA more broadly compares macro–micro explanations across work, education and households.

Both study population health, social determinants, health inequalities and empirical evidence. UCR adds epidemiological risk, study designs and a local public-health project; UvA centres sociological explanations and comparisons.

Both develop statistical inference, software analysis and empirical reporting. UCR extends into multivariable and experimental models; UvA introduces these statistical foundations through its earlier sociological survey data.

Both examine racialised power, intersecting identities, oppression and resistance. UCR centres American media and cultural history; UvA systematically connects race, gender and sexuality to epistemology, political economy and contemporary fascist forces.

Classical and contemporary theory also runs through the UCR sociology courses, but no additional selected course is counted as UvA’s distinct first theoretical foundation in interaction and social order.
No selected course develops the dedicated evolutionary and complexity account of cultural change, cooperation and human social organisation.
Research ethics and reflexivity occur elsewhere, but no selected course develops this distinct survey of social-science epistemology, ontology and philosophy.

UCR’s qualitative course includes interviewing, observation and a team project and is placed with qualitative analysis. No additional selected course is counted as this separately assessed introductory Amsterdam field project.

Migration and solidarity appear in sociology, conflict and global-relations courses. No selected course supplies the sustained migration, citizenship and integration theory and evidence of this dedicated component.
Social inequality, institutions and place recur in the alternatives, but no selected course centres urban social theory and urban inequality as this component does.
Modern Sociology includes Bourdieu and related work, but no additional selected course centres the dedicated culture–structure theoretical debate.
This thirty-credit elective space remains genuinely open, subject to the entry and registration conditions of the eventual choices.

Quantitative and qualitative inquiry are both available at UCR, including mixed-method foundations, but no selected course specifically develops their epistemological and analytical integration at this depth.

UCR includes several supervised research and writing projects, but no scheduled course supplies this individual eighteen-credit sociological thesis. Optional independent research remains additional to the scheduled programme.

selection.assessment: The closest programme uses the complete available UCR sociology sequence and a strong mixed-method social-research spine. The institution/policy and migration/race/global-society directions are independently supported by generator-eligible programme interests and the official curriculum, produce substantively different course choices, and pass feasibility and pairwise distinctness. Production therefore stops at the three-alternative maximum.

notes.text: UvA combines four dedicated theory courses, six sociological domains, an integrated qualitative–quantitative methods sequence and an individual eighteen-credit thesis. UCR provides a substantial sociology core with related historical, political, legal, psychological and empirical study. Dedicated migration, urban sociology and mixed-method integration remain differences; the relationships shown are partial.

audience.programmeDescription: Sociology at the University of Amsterdam examines social relations, inequality, institutions and change. Its English pathway combines sociological theory and craft with six subject domains, qualitative and quantitative research, thirty free-choice credits and an individual bachelor thesis.
audience.comparisonExplanation: UCR can emphasise sociology and empirical inequality research, institutional policy and collective action, or race, gender and global social relations. Each combines a substantial sociology core with specific related fields. UvA offers a more continuous disciplinary sequence, including dedicated migration and urban sociology, mixed-method integration and a larger individual thesis. The relationships shown are partial.
